newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodia faces painful cuts to bloated bureaucracy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodia faces painful cuts to bloated bureaucracy.

text.p: The dock workers toiling around the cranes and cargo under the blistering sun at Sihanoukville port could have the best government jobs in Cambodia.
At an average of $140 per month, they make seven times more than the average civil servant, and they are paid more if they perform better than expected.
They have a year-end bonus, job security, a health care plan for themselves and their families, and workers' compensation.
Their boss, port director Lou Kim Chhun, makes only one and a half times their salary.
"We live in the port like one family," he told Reuters. "We have very good relations."
The merits of a shallow bureaucracy and generous job benefits -- hallmarks of the port's innovative reform efforts -- are unfamiliar in Cambodia.

While other nations are painfully seeking to reinvent government in the face of harsh new economic realities, Cambodia has continued to burden its budget with a bloated civil service, which now numbers more than 150,000 people.
With the average government salary less than $20 and often late in coming, productivity is low and corruption high.
An afternoon walk through a government ministry can be a lonely experience -- much of the staff has left for their second jobs -- and morale is notoriously low.
But that is set to change.
International donors, who bankroll 40 percent of Cambodia's national budget, have grown weary of watching the civil servant numbers grow each year. Government economists agree reform is needed.

"The government has been carrying on a policy of pacification. The government will take more people on the payroll to strengthen various political parties," said senior government economist Seanglim Bit.
The private sector does not employ enough workers to reduce the demand for government jobs, which will make civil service reform very difficult, he said.
"This is a very, very big adjustment for the society. People are used to being trained to work for the state, with a lifelong employment guarantee," Seanglim Bit said.
"They were trained to be technocrats, and now they are expected to read the minds of entrepreneurs... we're operating in two separate cultures."
In a sign change may be imminent, Finance Minister Keat Chhon recently told international donors the government lacked budgetary discipline.
He decried the growing number of civil servants, which he said had increased by 5,000 in the past three years.
Officials announced a plan to reduce the civil ranks and the oversized armed forces, but said it would cost $150 million.
Reform also will be needed to streamline the civil service, and the port may have one solution.
Lou Kim Chhun faced a similar situation in 1992 when underpaid workers stole massive amounts of freight and ships took days to unload.
"They would take anything: spare parts, cement, fertiliser... If you wanted to export cargo, you had to meet at least 12 people," he told Reuters.
So he streamlined operations, reduced the bureaucracy and paid according to employee performance -- at far higher rates.
Workers eventually stopped stealing and ships are now unloaded in times competitive with Ho Chi Minh City's port in Vietnam, he said, despite Sinhanoukville's antiquated equipment.
"People should believe time is money. If we don't work, we lose customers. We found this is the best way," he said.
But Lou Kim Chhun knows reform is not easy. Despite protests, the government recently sent him 39 workers to add to his payroll, cutting into the port's efficiency.
"It won't be easy for the government," he said, noting the pressure to pad payrolls despite the need for reform. "They have bigger staffs and bigger problems." But he has proved it can be done.
